desc: THE EVENT THE LITERATURE CONFLATES WITH ECHO FLIGHT, SEPARATED HERE SO THAT EACH CAN BE GRADED HONESTLY. Robert Salas states that while on duty as deputy missile combat crew commander in the Oscar Flight launch control capsule at Malmstrom he took a call from a topside security policeman reporting a glowing red object hovering over the front gate, and that within moments the flight's missiles went off alert one after another. His commander was Lt, later Col., Frederick Meiwald. For years this was told as part of the 16 March 1967 Echo Flight event, which allowed Echo Flight's Tier 1 documentation to be read as corroborating it. Robert Hastings now places Oscar Flight on 24 March 1967, eight days later, on Capt. Robert Jamison's recollection of a second retargeting call-out, and states that Salas agrees the incidents were probably on separate days. THE SEPARATION IS WHAT MAKES THE HONEST GRADING POSSIBLE AND IT ALSO REMOVES THE DOCUMENTARY SUPPORT. Once the two events are distinct, the released unit history touches Echo Flight and says nothing whatever about Oscar Flight. A full-text search of the 88 released pages returns zero occurrences of 'Oscar', 'O Flight', '24 Mar' and '25 Mar'. This node is admitted under CLAUDE.md section 2a on notability and is carried at Tier 2, openly, as a named man's account on dated records.

dossier.narrative:
The zero count is the fact this node exists to state. A full-text search of the 88 released pages of the 341st Strategic Missile Wing histories, covering 1 January 1967 to 31 March 1968, returns zero occurrences of 'Oscar' and zero of 'O Flight'.

And the node immediately bounds its own strongest fact, which is the part most accounts on either side omit. The Air Force letter of 14 June 2001 describes the release as copies of excerpts and supporting documents of five quarterly histories, not the complete histories. A zero count in an excerpt is weaker than a zero count in a complete record, and saying so is the difference between evidence and rhetoric.

The date itself is worth following. 24 March 1967 is what separates Oscar from Echo, and it comes from Robert Hastings on Capt. Robert Jamison's information, with Salas agreeing the two incidents probably occurred on separate days. So the distinction that makes this a second event rests on testimony relayed through the field's principal aggregator, which is exactly the provenance question section 2a of CLAUDE.md now requires every such node to record.

James Carlson disputes that any Oscar Flight incident occurred at all, citing SAC UFO officer Col. Lewis D. Chase as finding no equipment failures or sighting on that date. He is the son of an Echo Flight officer and he argues this publicly and at length.

One document would move this node more than any other and it has not been opened by anyone here: Col. Frederick Meiwald's letter to Salas of 1 October 1996. Two incompatible characterisations of what it says are in circulation, one supporting Salas and one not. Until somebody opens it, the board carries both and endorses neither.

dossier.whatItIs: Robert Salas's claimed second Minuteman shutdown at Malmstrom AFB, dated 24 March 1967, eight days after the documented Echo Flight shutdown. It is a separate node from Echo Flight on purpose, because the literature conflates the two constantly and the documentary position of each is completely different.
dossier.whyImplicated: It is the cleanest test case this board has for the difference between a documented event and an attested one. Echo Flight is in the wing's own history in detail. Oscar Flight is not in it at all. Both are carried, correctly labelled, and neither borrows the other's weight. A reader who arrives believing 'the Air Force documented UFOs shutting down missiles' should be able to see exactly which half of that sentence the paper supports.
